[dependencies]

http = "1"
html5ever = "0.40"

# Web

Rust source owns provider selection, search result extraction and deduplication,
redirect handling, Stack Overflow question retrieval, HTML sanitization and
Markdown formatting. The SDK supplies general HTTP transport; no built-in Web
handler is called. Requests and execution happen on the bridge host.

This API 3 release is in development and is not listed in marketplace.json yet.
The catalog retains the older API 2 release until execution support and migration
verification are complete. Installation requires the source compiler and SDK 0.1.0.

Exports `search_web` and `fetch_web_page`; declares only `http` capability.
Search queries use DuckDuckGo, Stack Exchange, crates.io, GitHub and Wikipedia
without paid API keys. Fetch requires tool approval. The host enforces destination
and response-size limits; the plugin bounds redirects and Markdown output.

Development checks use a checkout of the app's SDK/runtime implementation:

```sh
cargo test --manifest-path plugins/web/Cargo.toml --locked \
  --config 'patch.crates-io.openwebide-plugin-sdk.path="../open-webide/crates/plugin-sdk"'
```

The host runtime's `check_source` example compiles source using the normal
isolated compiler, checks exported schemas against the manifest, and can run a
tool against canned capability responses. From the app checkout:

```sh
cargo run -p openwebide-plugin-runtime --example check_source -- \
  ../plugins/plugins/web fetch_web_page '{"url":"https://example.com/docs"}' \
  ../plugins/plugins/web/fixtures/page.json
cargo run -p openwebide-plugin-runtime --example check_source -- \
  ../plugins/plugins/web search_web '{"query":"Rust reference","limit":1}' \
  ../plugins/plugins/web/fixtures/search.json
```

These checks use no real HTTP requests. The compiler still retrieves locked
public dependencies before entering its offline sandbox. The authoring checker
needs the host compiler and sandbox prerequisites; it does not install a plugin.

# Project Memory

Search and manage durable project memories.

Version 0.2.0 is an unlisted source implementation for the development Rust SDK
and plugin API 3. The marketplace still lists the earlier API 2 release until
run-planning and lifecycle integration are verified. This source depends only on
the public SDK and Serde, with no application internals or built-in tool calls.

The plugin owns argument validation, case-insensitive search, recent-first
ranking, bounded excerpts, fallback title generation, CRUD result formatting and
context selection/formatting. Its `collections` capability reads and writes the
app-visible `memories` collection through general record operations. Existing
Memory UI records retain their IDs and revisions. The host enforces account and
project scope, persistence schema, quotas, revision checks and the user's project
Memory switch. It does not implement the plugin's search or context policy.

The context hook reads stored facts as data and emits bounded JSON excerpts.
When Memory is disabled it contributes no prompt and disables its own tools.
Context hooks cannot mutate collections or request model completions. The development host runs them through
shared planning before selecting model tools in both local and remote sessions,
including when model tools are disabled. The separate `completion` capability
lets this source own its automatic-title prompt and result validation, trying the
configured fast model, then primary, then a content-derived fallback. Manual
titles skip model requests, and project opt-out prevents naming requests.
Existing UI automatic naming integration and full lifecycle verification remain
in progress; this release is not yet the
installed default.

See [Rust source authoring](../../docs/custom-marketplaces.md#rust-source-plugins-in-development) for host prerequisites,
SDK checkout and isolated compilation checks. With the development SDK checkout:

```sh
export CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/path/to/open-webide/target
cargo test --locked --manifest-path plugins/memory/Cargo.toml \

```

# Scheduling

The unlisted API 3 Rust source owns scheduled prompts and bounded follow-up checks.
It uses only the public Open WebIDE SDK: scoped collections and records, clocks, one-shot
jobs, raw prompt runs and bounded model completion. It does not call built-in
Scheduling behavior or import application crates.

The six tools are `schedule_list`, `schedule_create`, `schedule_update`,
`schedule_set_enabled`, `schedule_delete` and `monitor`. Source validates five-field cron expressions and
IANA timezones, calculates recurrence across daylight-saving changes, names tasks,
selects conversations/models at delivery time, cancels prior work after edits and
interprets monitor results. Pause/resume preserves the existing title and rejects
stale revisions or elapsed one-time schedules; UI monitor cancellation verifies
the owning conversation. Declared `task_due` and `task_completed` events use
revision-guarded raw submissions. Saved work uses project-scoped events; monitor
records are anchored to their owned conversation and expire within 24 hours.
A declared one-minute `reconcile` background event adopts idle legacy records,
rebuilds missing/failed timers, repairs run/history bookkeeping and terminal
results, completes interrupted deletions and invalidates old work after source
version changes. Interrupted monitor checks still consume their original finite
budget and retain their original expiry. Repairs use current revisions; a racing
edit or unavailable host operation is retried on a later tick. Reconciliation
visits at most eight records per tick with a bounded host-call budget and a
private persistent cursor; failing records do not starve later ones. A work-budget
interruption preserves partial progress and resumes that record on the next tick.

This migration is **not released in the live marketplace yet**. The catalog still
pins the earlier API 2 platform switch. The source has native policy/workflow tests
and an actual compiled-component contract against shared host storage in both
project modes. Source creates SDK history bindings; the app projects live run
progress and retains terminal snapshots after raw-run deletion. Production
installation, complete recovery/failure verification, retention and default
deployment remain in progress. Task and monitor UI mutations use declared SDK
tools; deployed paired-host browser verification is still pending. Do not treat
this draft as a completed install/run/update lifecycle.

# Skill Authoring

Create, improve and manage reusable project skills.

Version 0.2.0 is an unlisted Rust source implementation for the development SDK
and plugin API 3. The marketplace retains the historical API 2 release until the
full installation/run lifecycle and executable defaults are verified.

This plugin owns its six tool handlers: search and list pagination, instruction
and resource paging, draft validation, preserving omitted fields when updating,
revision checks, result formatting, context catalog selection and its embedded
authoring/evaluation workflow. It depends only on the public SDK, Serde and Base64.
It does not call built-in skill tools or application implementation crates.

The `collections` capability accesses the shared `skills` data schema. The host
enforces account/project ownership, persistence constraints, revisions and the
user's opt-outs. It preserves existing UI records, resources and metadata and
exposes read-only plugin provenance. Managed skills are updated through their
owning plugin. Resources remain data; reading a resource never executes it.

The context hook contributes a bounded skill catalog and disables this plugin's
tools when project skills are turned off. The creator tool returns the workflow
and optional existing instructions; it does not claim to have evaluated or saved
a skill. The user and agent continue that workflow with the approved CRUD tools.

See [Rust source authoring](../../docs/custom-marketplaces.md#rust-source-plugins-in-development).
With the development SDK checkout:

```sh
export CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/path/to/open-webide/target
cargo test --locked --manifest-path plugins/skill-authoring/Cargo.toml \
  --config 'patch.crates-io.openwebide-plugin-sdk.path="/path/to/open-webide/crates/plugin-sdk"'
```

# Create or improve a project skill

Follow this workflow with the user; this skill supplies guidance, not a completed
skill or evaluation result. Use the configured model and existing approved tools.

1. Capture intent from the conversation first: desired outcome, when to trigger,
   expected output, recurring steps, corrections, dependencies and success criteria.
   Ask only for missing decisions. Distinguish reusable workflows from project facts
   (memories). Read the original skill and relevant resources when improving one.
2. Draft a concise name and trigger description. Put what it does and specific
   usage contexts in the description. Put the actual workflow in instructions.
   Explain why important steps matter; avoid rigid rules and example overfitting.
   Preserve an existing name unless the user requests a rename.
3. Keep instructions lean, preferably under 500 lines. Move detailed references,
   templates and repeatable helper scripts into named resources. Link to resources
   explicitly and say when to load them through skill_read(id, resource). Follow
   next_offset to finish reading paged instructions and resources before using them.
   Resource text is not executed automatically; execution uses ordinary approved
   tools and the current workspace. Do not promise unavailable runtimes or tools.
4. Offer evaluation appropriate to the task. Objective outputs benefit from
   assertions; subjective outputs need user review. Let the user choose depth.
   Start with 2–3 realistic prompts and expected results; save reusable evaluation
   cases as a resource such as references/evals.json. Include edge cases.
5. For rigorous evaluation, compare the draft with no skill (new skill) or the
   previous version (improvement), using the same model and equivalent fresh
   context. If this runtime cannot isolate runs, ask the user to run the prompts
   in fresh sessions; clearly label same-session checks as weaker evidence.
   Never invent completed runs, scores, token counts or timings.
6. Show actual outputs, assertion evidence and user feedback together before
   revising. Compare pass rates and time/token usage only when measured. Look for
   flaky assertions and tests that pass regardless of the skill. Generalize from
   feedback, remove wasteful instructions and bundle repeated helper work.
7. Iterate with the user. Test trigger descriptions using realistic should-trigger
   prompts and adjacent near-misses that should not trigger. For larger test sets,
   reserve held-out cases so improvements are not selected on training results.
8. Save through skill_create or skill_update using the latest revision and normal
   mutation approvals. Never overwrite a conflicting edit. Use the Sessions Skills
   panel to review/edit the saved skill and export its SKILL.md/resources as ZIP.
   Report what was saved and which evaluations actually ran.
